Hundreds of public hospitals in Romania went on an all-out strike on Tuesday. Negotiations between healthcare trade unions and the relevant ministry are continuing, with no concrete outcome following the first round of talks. In the absence of guarantees that their demands will be met, the SANITAS Federation has announced that the general strike will not be called off. Trade unionists from the Federation are protesting against the draft bill – still under debate – for the new law on a unified pay scale for public sector staff, and are calling for measures to resolve the problems within the healthcare system – the staff shortage, which affects both staff performance and the quality of services provided to patients, as well as the prospect of cuts to certain allowances. The protesters are therefore calling for vacant posts to be filled, better working conditions and a pay law that reflects the responsibility and complexity of work within the healthcare system. Parliament. On Tuesday, the Budget Committee of the Chamber of Deputies in Bucharest issued a favourable report on the draft bill to approve the SAFE Loan Agreement between the European Union and Romania, worth 16,680,055,394 euros. The draft is due to be debated in the plenary session of the Chamber of Deputies, the first chamber to consider it, and will then be sent to the Senate, which is the decision-making body. According to the draft, the servicing of the public debt relating to the loan – namely the repayment of the principal, the payment of financing costs, liquidity management costs, administrative costs and other costs associated with the loan – will be covered by the Ministry of Finance, in accordance with the legislation in force. Drones. Romania considers that Russia bears responsibility for the drones shot down in its national airspace, Acting Foreign Minister Oana Ţoiu stated at a press conference on Tuesday. She added that Romania had taken a ‘clear, firm’ stance, which included summoning the Russian ambassador to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, where he was shown fragments of one of the three drones recently shot down in Romanian airspace, as well as the results of the investigation confirming that the drone was Russian. Oana Ţoiu recalled that NATO had reaffirmed its support for Bucharest, as well as the fact that Romania is a state that does not negotiate its borders and does not permit illegal entry into its airspace. We recall that at the end of last week there were three incidents involving drones that illegally entered Romania’s airspace. Agreement. The Romanian company Oves Enterprise and Edrone, one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers, have signed a strategic partnership laying the foundation for the joint production of military drones in Cluj-Napoca (north-western Romania). “Europe needs its own production capabilities and Romania must build a genuine industrial role within this ecosystem rather than remaining solely a sales market,” said Oves Enterprise in a press statement issued on Tuesday. In the initial phase, three types of military drone will be manufactured in Cluj-Napoca, namely FPV, interceptor and reconnaissance. The range of products may later be expanded to include up to 27 models. Initial production capacity will be approximately 1,000 units per month, with hopes of increasing this to between 10,000 and 15,000 units monthly. Visit. On Thursday, Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan will welcome his counterpart from the Republic of Moldova (a former Soviet republic with a predominantly Romanian-speaking population), Vasile Tofan, to Bucharest. This will be Mr Tofan’s first official visit to Romania since taking office. The agenda for the talks includes ways to accelerate bilateral projects, with a focus on those in the transport and energy sectors, designed to help ensure greater interconnectivity between the two banks of the Prut River and to address current challenges. The two senior officials will also address issues relating to the security situation in the region, against the backdrop of Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and the security and economic consequences of this war. Prime Minister Bolojan will reiterate Romania’s firm support for the Republic of Moldova’s accession to the EU and will discuss specific aspects of assistance and diplomatic and sectoral coordination to advance this process. Firefighters. Romania has extended the mission of the firefighter contingent deployed to southwestern France by another two weeks to assist French and international teams in extinguishing devastating wildfires and forest fires. According to a government statement, the decision reflects Bucharest’s solidarity with its European partners and its commitment to contributing to emergency management within the framework of the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism. Recently, French President Emmanuel Macron posted a message on X thanking the Romanian firefighters for their assistance in battling the fires. Survey. Around 70 per cent of Romanians living abroad for at least seven months a year rule out returning to the country in the coming year, although the majority have already made investments in Romania, according to an opinion poll published on Tuesday. The socio-professional profile of Romanians living abroad indicates significant structural stability, with 44 per cent of them in employment and 23 per cent working as managers or entrepreneurs. Romanians in the UK have the most advanced economic profile, with 29 per cent of respondents holding leadership or entrepreneurial roles, 62 per cent having a university degree, and 46 per cent earning over 3,000 euros a month. Over 60 per cent of Romanian citizens in the diaspora say they have invested considerable sums in Romania, either by providing financial support to families who have remained in the country, or in property or small businesses run by relatives. The community in Germany has the highest investment rate: 71 per cent, and the highest level of direct financial support for family: 44 per cent. Anthem Day. National Anthem Day will be celebrated on Wednesday with military ceremonies taking place at all garrisons across Romania. In Bucharest, the event will take place in Tricolor Square. The programme includes a religious service, a presentation on the meaning and symbolism of the anthem’s lyrics, and a concert performed by the Ministry of Defence’s Representative Band. National Anthem Day was established by law in 1998 and is celebrated every year on 29 July. “Awaken, Romanian!” was composed by Anton Pann, and the lyrics were written by the poet Andrei Mureșanu. https://www.politico.eu/article/french-c.text: PARIS — Senior representatives for France’s feuding centrist presidential candidates are sitting down for lunch Wednesday to figure out who is best placed to take on Marine Le Pen in the spring 2027 election race to replace Emmanuel Macron. But a compromise that could save the political center from being crushed by the extremes doesn’t look like it’s on the menu. Supporters of Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, two of Macron’s former prime ministers courting similar voters, are growing increasingly anxious that the duo’s internecine duel will drag on so long that it will damage the centrist camp’s chances. Advertisement Advertisement Without a strong candidate from the center, their fear is that the election will slide inexorably into a clash between two anti-NATO euroskeptics who frighten financial markets: Le Pen on the far right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the far left. The presidential election goes to a runoff if no one secures more than 50 percent of the vote. Le Pen appears all but certain to nab one of those spots given her polling numbers, but Mélenchon’s strong start to the campaign means he could well score ahead of Philippe and secure a spot in the second round. Playing the long game Despite the pressure to find a real challenger to Le Pen, the squabbling centrists hardly appear in a hurry to resolve their differences. Attal, who trails Philippe in the polls, has in recent days tried to frame Philippe as out of touch . Asked about the remarks, Philippe responded that candidates sharing the center ground should direct their attacks against the extremes. Attal’s campaign director Franck Riester told a small group of reporters Tuesday he doesn’t expect a resolution before February. Philippe said in an interview Tuesday he didn’t think a single candidate would emerge before next year. Instead, Wednesday’s lunch — the latest in a series of regular parleys among the centrists — will be a moment to “air grievances,” according to Riester. Advertisement Advertisement “We will continue to discuss the campaign, ways to avoid inflicting irreparable damage [on each other], and agree on a code of conduct,” he said. Attal and his advisers started organizing the meetings in the spring, after Philippe launched his campaign but before Attal’s announcement, to ensure the centrist bloc remained united. But the encounters have been marred by disagreements over how to rally around a single champion. A lawmaker from Philippe’s party, Horizons, concurred that Tuesday’s meeting would not lead to a breakthrough. Portrait of Marine Le Pen during La REF of MEDEF at Roland Garros in Paris, on August 27, 2026. | Mael Ghazi/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images “We are going because we are polite but we’ve never believed in it,” said the MP, who was, like others quoted in this story, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Ruinous infighting While polls suggest Philippe is among the best-placed candidates to mount a serious challenge to Le Pen, the plethora of hopefuls in the political center is allowing the two anti-establishment candidates to dominate the public discourse on everything from banning the hijab to writing off massive chunks of French debt. One former centrist minister said that “internal competition” between Philippe and Attal, who are the closest ideologically, could end up destroying a centrist bloc that already faces an uphill battle given voter dissatisfaction with Macron’s presidency. Advertisement Advertisement “The risk is that the winner ends up ruling over a wasteland,” said the former minister. Given the increasing difficulties in reaching an agreement with Attal’s camp, some Philippe supporters are hoping for an alliance with the once-dominant conservative Les Républicains, which Philippe once belonged to. The party’s candidate, Bruno Retailleau, is trailing Attal and Philippe in the polls. But an alliance there too seems elusive. Retailleau last week said he would keep on campaigning “until victory.” In any case, he wasn’t even invited to the lunch. Sarah Paillou contributed reporting.

Sign up here Martin Belam Mon 12 Oct 2026 07.38 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said it was “news to me” after Donald Trump announced a partial ceasefire deal in the Ukraine war. The US president had posted to social media to say: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed.” There was no sign that the Kremlin was observing Trump’s ceasefire. According to Zelenskyy, Russian drones took to the sky “throughout the day” on Sunday and there were several airstrikes, including on energy infrastructure. He said Russia hit a power station in Kharkiv – the latest of more than 200 strikes during the past week against electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine. How has the prospect of a deal been welcomed? Despite the unconventional nature of the announcement, the ceasefire appeared to garner support from Ukraine’s key western allies. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said Paris supported a “real energy ceasefire” and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said a sustained energy ceasefire was “the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets”. Will Trump’s deal with Putin bring down gas prices? The agreement to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted . Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats must ‘win by massive numbers’ to fend off Trump election denial View image in fullscreen Abdul El-Sayed said Donald Trump and the president’s Republicans allies were ‘bound to try to sow doubt about the integrity of the results’. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Democrats must “win by massive numbers” during November’s federal midterm elections because Donald Trump and his Republican allies are bound to try to sow doubt about the integrity of the results, the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said on Sunday . “Donald Trump has already threatened to do what he did in 2020, which is deny the outcomes of an election,” El-Sayed said. “So, yes, we have to win by massive numbers.” Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say View image in fullscreen An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 of King Khalid airport, killing one person and injuring 11 others on Sunday. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety View image in fullscreen Brad Smith said AI could be a ‘tool and a weapon’ that should be regulated urgently. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said , as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI. Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents. There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow. Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently. US maternity wards face wave of closures as Medicaid cuts kick in View image in fullscreen According to analysis by Protect Our Care, 52 maternity wards have closed since the HR1 bill was announced in July 2025. Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters Maternity wards across the US are facing a wave of closures as cuts to federal Medicaid funding take effect, experts have said. According to analysis by the nonprofit Protect Our Care, 52 maternity wards have closed since the HR1 bill was announced in July 2025, with a further eight having announced their upcoming closure. The legislation, which comes into full effect in the new year, will result in many adults covered through Medicaid having to meet new work requirements and being subject to more frequent eligibility checks, while there will be less federal funding for states for Medicaid. Republican Christopher Paul, accused of child rape, is on course to become police chief in small Louisiana town. He is running unopposed for the seat despite allegations he raped two girls 20 years ago. The Beach Boys’ Mike Love has returned to the stage , aged 85, despite being described as “facing serious health challenges”. A wildlife park in Yorkshire, England, has confirmed the tiger that mauled to death a man who entered its enclosure will not be euthanised . The man, who has not yet been named, was seen entering the enclosure before police were called on Saturday. She says the government should also “jump on the phone” with the big tech companies to stop them allowing the stream on their platforms. The eSafety commissioner revealed overnight she did not have the powers to proactively prevent the stream from being shown or accessed in Australia. She adds, if the laws need to be fixed to prevent the live stream – or any future live stream – that should be done. I mean, this is barbaric … the idea that a state-sanctioned killing would be televised, would be livestreamed as content, almost for entertainment value, as a government PR episode.
